videos.title: MLP · Vectors in, vectors out
videos.description: At the vector level, with no maths: the one vector that comes in from attention, the detectors the MLP holds (a pattern and a write-back each, learned once and fixed), how detecting and writing back work, and what comes out.

videos.title: MLP 1 · Step by step
videos.description: What the MLP does for each token after attention, then its three steps for “it”: expand into detectors, bend with GELU, shrink back and add.

videos.title: MLP 2 · GELU, SwiGLU and memory
videos.description: ReLU, GELU and SiLU side by side, the gate in SwiGLU, what the MLP stores as keys and values, where the parameters are, and mixture of experts explained simply.

slides.title: The big idea: each token thinks on its own
slides.summary: After attention, every token goes through the same small network, by itself. Most of the model's parameters, and much of what it knows, live here.
body: Every transformer layer has two parts. Attention moves information between tokens. The MLP (multi-layer perceptron, also called the feed-forward layer) then works on each token's vector on its own.

ul: Same network, every token. One set of weights per layer, applied to each token separately, so all tokens can run at once.
No mixing. The MLP never looks at other tokens. Anything it needs from them, attention brought in first.
Three steps: expand into thousands of detectors, bend them with an activation, shrink back and add. The next three slides take them one at a time.

body: <mark>Attention gathers context from other tokens. The MLP works out what that context means for this token.</mark>

body.note: Attention is the group discussion. The MLP is each person thinking it over alone.

body.more: Why is it called a multi-layer perceptron?
body.text: A perceptron is the classic artificial neuron: weigh the inputs, add them up, decide. Two layers of them with a bend in between make an MLP. Transformers use exactly this shape, just very wide.

viz.html: The same design at two sizes. The MLP's middle is always several times wider than the token.

figure.alt: One transformer layer for “The cat sat on the mat because it”. First, attention moves information between tokens: “it” takes in some of “cat”. Then the same small MLP runs on every token separately, with no mixing between tokens. Each MLP's output is added back to its token. The three steps inside: expand 768 numbers to 3,072 detector scores, bend them with GELU so only the detectors that fired stay strong, then shrink back to 768 and add to the token.
figure.caption: Attention mixes between tokens; the MLP runs on each token separately, then adds its result back.

slides.title: Vectors in, vectors out: what the MLP holds
slides.summary: The MLP gets one vector per token, compares it with thousands of learned patterns, and adds back what the matching ones write.
body: What goes in is one vector per token: 768 numbers in GPT-2. For “it”, that's the word itself plus what attention blended in from “cat”: a pronoun, an animal, the one that sat.
Its parameters: 3,072 detectors per layer, learned in training and then fixed. Each detector is just two vectors of 768 numbers:

ul: A write-back ✍: what it adds when it fires.
Detect: the token's vector is compared with every pattern. If the two line up, that detector fires.
Write back: each firing detector adds its write-back, scaled by how strongly it fired. Together they make one new vector, added to “it”.

body: <mark>Parameters (the patterns and write-backs) are learned once and then fixed; vectors (the token's own numbers) are new for every token, every time.</mark>

body.note: For “it”, the detector whose pattern is “a pronoun pointing to an animal” fires, and writes back something like “this is the cat: alive, can get tired”. A detector looking for “a date” stays quiet.

body.text: Comparing is a dot product of the token's vector with each pattern. The 3,072 patterns are the columns of the first matrix (768 × 3,072), and the write-backs are the rows of the second (3,072 × 768). That's 768 × 3,072 × 2 ≈ 4.7 million weights per layer.

viz.html: One MLP layer of GPT-2. Orange = parameters, learned once. Blue = vectors, new every time.

figure.alt: Three panels. In: one vector per token, 768 numbers; for “it” it carries a pronoun, an animal and the one that sat, from attention; it is new for every token. Inside, the MLP’s parameters, learned once and fixed: 3,072 detectors per layer, each a pattern (what it looks for) and a write-back (what it adds). Shown: “pronoun → animal” and “a living thing”, whose patterns line up with “it”, and “a date”, whose pattern doesn’t. The steps: compare with each pattern, keep the ones that fire, add their write-backs. Out: a vector of the same size, now also saying “this is the cat: alive, can get tired”, passed to the next layer. Parameters are learned once; vectors are new for every token, every time.
figure.caption: One vector in, thousands of fixed detectors inside, one richer vector out.

slides.title: Step 1: expand into detectors
slides.summary: A matrix turns each token's vector into thousands of scores, one per detector.
body: The first matrix multiplies the token's vector up to a much wider one: from 768 numbers to 3,072 in GPT-2. Each of those numbers is a detector (often called a neuron): one row of the matrix, scoring how strongly one pattern is present.

ul: A high score: the pattern is there.
Nobody picks the patterns. Training finds useful ones: a topic, a grammar rule, a kind of word, a fact.

body: <mark>Going wider gives the model room to check for thousands of patterns at once.</mark>

body.note: In the toy on the right, each token has 4 numbers and there are 6 named detectors. For “it”, which already took in some “cat” through attention, “a pronoun for an animal” scores 1.52 and “a living thing” 0.34. The others score below −1.

body.text: No. Real neurons often respond to several unrelated things at once, because a model packs in more patterns than it has neurons. Researchers call this superposition, and build tools to pull clean features back out. The labels here are for teaching.

slides.title: Step 2: bend, with an activation function
slides.summary: Each score goes through a curve that keeps the detectors that fired and quietens the rest.
body: Next, every score passes through the same simple curve, the activation function. GPT-2 uses GELU: strong positive scores pass almost unchanged, negative ones are squashed close to 0.

Two matrix multiplications in a row are the same as one. Without a bend between them, the MLP, and the whole stack of layers, would collapse into one straight-line function, however many layers it had.
<mark>The bend lets the model make decisions, like “only if this pattern is here”, and so learn complicated things.</mark>

body.note: Switch between GELU and ReLU on the right. ReLU cuts every negative score to exactly 0. GELU lets a little through: for “it”, “a pronoun for an object” scores −1.00 and comes out as −0.16.

slides.title: Step 3: shrink back, and add
slides.summary: A second matrix turns the detectors that fired into a small change, which is added to the token's vector.
body: The second matrix shrinks the wide vector back to the model's width (3,072 → 768 in GPT-2). Each detector has its own row in it: a small vector it writes back when it fires, scaled by how strongly it fired.
That result doesn't replace the token's vector. It's added to it, through the residual connection, so the token keeps what it had and gains what the MLP worked out.
<mark>The MLP's output is a small edit to each token's vector, not a new vector.</mark>

body.note: Run “it” on the right. “A pronoun for an animal” fires and writes “animal”, so the MLP adds +0.77 to the animal number: 0.60 becomes 1.37. With attention's help, “it” now reads as the cat.

body.text: Adding keeps every earlier layer's work in the vector, and gives training an easy path back to the early layers.

slides.title: ReLU, GELU and SiLU
slides.summary: Three popular curves. They agree on big positive numbers and differ just below zero.
body: Every activation keeps strong positive signals and weakens negative ones. They differ in how:

ul: ReLU: anything below 0 becomes exactly 0. Simple and fast, but a detector stuck below zero gets no learning signal and can stay off for good (a “dead neuron”).
GELU (GPT-2, BERT): smooth. It scales each number by a factor that goes gently from 0, for big negatives, to 1, for big positives. Small negatives leak through a little.
SiLU, also called Swish: the same idea with a slightly different curve. It's the one inside SwiGLU, on the next slide.

body: <mark>Smooth curves keep a small learning signal below zero, and in practice train a little better than ReLU.</mark>

body.note: Drag the slider on the right. At −1, ReLU gives 0, GELU −0.159 and SiLU −0.269. At 2, they give 2, 1.954 and 1.762.

slides.title: SwiGLU: a gate on every detector
slides.summary: Most modern models expand each token twice: one copy, passed through SiLU, decides how much of the other gets through.
body: Llama, Mistral, Qwen, DeepSeek and most open models today use SwiGLU, an MLP with a gate:

ul: Two expansions of the same token vector, side by side.
One goes through SiLU and becomes the gate. The other is the value.
They're multiplied number by number, so each gate sets how much of its value passes, from off to fully on. Then the result shrinks back as before.

body: <mark>With a gate, the model can control each signal precisely instead of just switching it on or off. In tests, this trains better than a plain MLP of the same size.</mark>
Three matrices instead of two means more weights, so the middle is made narrower to compensate. Llama 3 8B goes from 4,096 to 14,336 and back: 3.5× wide instead of 4×.

body.text: Noam Shazeer's 2020 paper “GLU Variants Improve Transformer” tried several gated versions, and SwiGLU and GeGLU did best. Google's PaLM and Meta's Llama adopted SwiGLU, and most open models followed. Gemma uses GeGLU: the same gate with GELU.

figure.alt: Two versions of the MLP. A plain MLP, as in GPT-2: expand the token's 768 numbers to 3,072, pass every number through GELU, then shrink back. SwiGLU, as in Llama, Mistral and Qwen: expand the token's vector twice, side by side. One copy goes through SiLU and becomes a gate; the other is the value. They are multiplied number by number, so each gate decides how much of its value passes, then the result shrinks back. SwiGLU has three matrices instead of two, so its middle is narrower: Llama 3 8B goes from 4,096 to 14,336, 3.5 times wider. GELU is used by GPT-2 and BERT, SwiGLU by Llama, Mistral and Qwen, and GeGLU, the same gate with GELU, by Gemma.
figure.caption: A plain MLP bends every number; SwiGLU lets a second copy of the expansion act as a gate.

slides.title: What the MLP stores
slides.summary: Research suggests the MLP works like a huge key–value memory. It also holds most of a model's parameters.
body: A 2021 study (Geva and colleagues) found a neat way to read the MLP. Each detector's row in the first matrix is a key that matches a pattern in the text. Its row in the second matrix is a value: what to add when that pattern shows up. Values often push up words likely to come next.
A 2022 study (Meng and colleagues) traced facts like “the Eiffel Tower is in Paris” to the MLPs of middle layers, and changed a fact by editing a single MLP's weights.
<mark>Much of what a model knows, from facts to word associations, is stored in its MLP weights.</mark>
The MLP has two or three big matrices; attention has four smaller ones. Per layer, the MLP holds two thirds of the weights in GPT-2 small, and about 81% in Llama 3 8B.

body.more: Mixture of experts: many MLPs, only a few run
text: Some models split each MLP into several smaller ones, called experts (say 8), plus a small router. For each token, the router picks the 2 experts that fit it best, and only those run.

Think of a hospital with 8 specialists: reception sends you to the 2 who fit your case, not to all 8. So the model can store a lot, but each token only pays for 2 experts. Mixtral 8x7B stores about 47 billion parameters but uses only about 13 billion for each token.
The experts aren't neatly “the maths expert” or “the French expert”: the router learns its own way of splitting the work.
body.link: Mixture of experts, in The transformer block

figure.alt: Left: the MLP as a key–value memory, for the text “The Eiffel Tower is in”. Each detector is a key: the one matching “Eiffel Tower” fires strongly, “a city name” fires a little, and unrelated ones such as “a fruit” and “a past action” stay silent. Each detector also has a value, what it writes back when it fires: the Eiffel Tower detector pushes “Paris” up, so the next token is likely “Paris”. Studies found facts like this in the MLPs of middle layers. Right: parameters per layer. GPT-2 small: attention 2.4 million, MLP 4.7 million, 67% in the MLP. Llama 3 8B: attention 41.9 million, MLP 176.2 million, 81% in the MLP. Detector strengths are illustrative; parameter counts are exact.
figure.caption: Detectors are keys, what they write back are values. And the MLP is where most of the weights are.
